analysis.one_liner: Creates a national health service providing health care to everyone in the United States.
analysis.headline: A bill to create a government-run national health service died in committee after its referral to three House committees and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Barbara Lee introduced the Josephine Butler United States Health Service Act in July 2007. It would have created an independent federal agency, the United States Health Service, charged with providing health care and supplemental health services to everyone in the country [S2]. That would have replaced private health insurance as the way Americans pay for care: no premiums, no deductibles, no networks. The bill was referred to three House committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means — and then to subcommittees in July and September 2007 [S1] [S5]. None of them ever took it up. It had only three cosponsors [S4]. When the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, the bill died without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Every resident of the United States would gain health coverage at no premium or out-of-pocket cost, and the bill text directs particular attention to underserved groups, the chronically ill, and services such as childbirth and self-help and mutual aid groups [S2] [S3]. People who are uninsured, underinsured, or denied coverage because of pre-existing conditions would benefit most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone in the U.S.; the uninsured most of all

how_it_helps.text: Establishes the United States Health Service, an independent executive branch entity, to provide health care and supplemental health services to all individuals within the United States.
Coverage would extend to everyone in the country, ending the link between health coverage and employment or insurance status.
The bill text provides for services including childbirth care (with prior informed consent) and support for self-help and mutual aid groups, and directs attention to the chronically ill.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the funding of a universal health system, and the private health insurance industry, whose product would be replaced by a government-run service. Employers who currently help pay premiums would shift to paying taxes instead, and pharmaceutical companies and hospitals would face a single government purchaser instead of many private insurers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and the private health insurance industry

drawbacks.text: A universal government-run health system would require a very large increase in federal spending and taxes; the CRS summary identifies no dedicated funding source beyond the general health service it establishes.
Replacing private insurance would end the coverage arrangements tens of millions of Americans currently have through employers, requiring a full transition to a new system.

Critics of single-payer and national-health-service models have long argued that a single government payer can limit patient choice of plans and constrain provider payments, raising concerns about access and wait times; the bill's text addresses refusal of services only in limited cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would have been universal coverage for everyone in the country, ending premiums, deductibles, and coverage denials. The cost would have been a major expansion of federal health spending and taxes and the elimination of the private insurance market as it exists. Whether that trade-off is worth it is a genuine political question — but the House never engaged with it, so voters never got an answer or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees and their subcommittees for the rest of the 110th Congress without a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 11, 2007 and referred the same day to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means.

It was then referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health (July 2007), and in September 2007 to the Education and Labor Subcommittee on Workforce Protections and the Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee.
The bill had only three cosponsors, all in the House, and no further action of any kind was taken before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, pharmaceutical companies, and other stakeholders in the employer-based insurance system are better off because the bill never advanced — no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever held on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private health insurers and the insurance status quo

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, and Democrats controlled the House at the time, but the bill never reached a floor vote where party lines could be counted.

industries.note: A national health service that covers everyone directly would replace private health insurance as the payment channel for American health care, ending the industry's core business of selling coverage and collecting premiums.
A single government payer for all Americans would have far more bargaining power over drug prices than millions of fragmented private insurers, threatening current pricing.
Providers would gain a guaranteed patient base with no unpaid care, but would lose private-insurance reimbursement rates and bill a single government payer instead.
Most employers would stop paying health insurance premiums, but would pay taxes to fund the system instead; small businesses that struggle most with coverage costs would gain the most.
